abstract: OpenAI economists with Columbia and Wharton co-authors (arXiv 2608.12236, August 2026) link ChatGPT Enterprise account records to usage, worker job titles, message-level task classifications and Compustat financials through March 2026. They document four facts. Enterprise usage grew rapidly: output tokens rose about sevenfold from June 2025 to March 2026, and about half of that growth came from deeper use inside already-adopting firms. Among US public companies, adopters are larger, more valuable, and more R&D- and SG&A-intensive. Use within adopting firms spans job functions and seniority levels, with early-career workers the most intensive users. Tasks span writing, communication, information synthesis, research, data analysis, legal and finance work.
keyFindings: ChatGPT Enterprise output tokens grew roughly sevenfold between June 2025 and March 2026, and nearly fourfold within firms that adopted between January 2024 and June 2025.
Adopting US public firms are much larger than non-adopters: median revenue $2,275.1M vs $209.6M; median employment 2,934 vs 424 workers.
Within industries, firms in the top revenue quartile are 7.2 percentage points more likely to adopt, and firms in the top 5% are 11.3 points more likely.
At the average adopting firm after six months, managers and directors are about 24% of weekly active users; early-career workers and trainees are 7%.
Early-career workers and trainees send roughly eight to nine more weekly messages than the average active user in the same firm.
methodology: Internal ChatGPT Enterprise data (organization-week usage panel; worker-level sample of over 1,500 organizations and over 17 million messages at the six-month adoption horizon), linked to job titles, privacy-preserving task classifiers, and Compustat for US public companies (410 adopter tickers with positive message volume vs 11,784 non-adopter tickers, from a random sample). Descriptive and conditional-association regressions; no causal design.
qualifiers: Tier 2: company research on its own product. The authors are OpenAI staff or paid OpenAI contractors, and the paper is an unrefereed working paper. It covers one vendor's enterprise product only; firms classed as non-adopters may use other AI tools. The public-company sample is a random draw chosen to limit commercial disclosure, so it yields no economy-wide adoption rate. Message volume measures intensity, not productivity.
